title: Surprise-Move
primitive: the small move that rotates the listener's expectation — the lawful surprise that earns the Turn
summary: A surprise that breaks the tale's logic feels like a trick. A surprise that obeys the tale's logic feels like a discovery. This kit listens for HOW the surprise lands at the Turn — whether the seed was planted in the Hook or the Setup, whether the Close honors the rotation. Phase 2 separates surprise-as-craft from surprise-as-twist.

questions.prompt: Tell a 60-second tale with a small surprise at the Turn. After you finish, ask yourself: which Hook or Setup detail planted the seed for the surprise? If nothing planted it, the surprise might be a trick instead of a discovery.
What's the strongest move when you want a surprise the listener will REMEMBER, not just notice?
options: Make the surprise huge — bigger than anything they expected.
Plant a small unrelated-seeming detail in the Hook, then have the Turn use it.
Tell the listener up front that a surprise is coming.
questions.rationale: Memory loves callbacks. A small Hook detail that returns at the Turn makes the surprise feel inevitable in retrospect — and inevitability is what listeners remember. Huge surprises with no setup feel like tricks; warning the listener removes the surprise.

questions.prompt: Pick a tale from your anthology where the Turn surprised the listener. Which earlier moment planted the seed? If you can't find one, where COULD you plant a seed if you re-told the tale tomorrow?

Take a tale where the Turn felt too sudden. Add ONE sentence to the Hook that plants a tiny seed — an image, an offhand line, a small object. Keep everything else the same. Read both versions aloud and listen for the difference at the Turn.

castCameos.line: The strongest surprises are pivots that the Hook already pointed at. The listener should feel the moment go: 'oh — THAT was the door all along.'
I lean in when a small Hook detail returns at the Turn. The shape clicks. That click is what listeners feel as 'good surprise.'
A held breath before the surprise is the cue. If you rush the Turn, the surprise lands but doesn't echo. Slowing makes the rotation visible.
Try repeating the planted detail TWICE before the Turn — once in the Hook, once in the Setup. By the third return at the Turn, the surprise is a homecoming.
